A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SoftMatcha 2 research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison across the substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original latency measurements, pruning ablations, multilingual search results, and manually verified benchmark-contamination findings.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds real-query evaluation, cache experiments, retrieval and paraphrase results, quality judgments, and empirical checks of theoretical assumptions.

M1.justification: The core suffix-array search, pruning techniques, similarity function, and adaptive thresholding remain. Appendix I adds document-scoring adaptations for downstream retrieval, including an explicitly tested IDF-weighted variant, Ours+IDF, for paraphrase source identification.

E1.justification: v2 adds ORCAS search queries, information retrieval on TREC-COVID and SciFact, and source-document identification using GPT-5.4 paraphrases of FineWeb-Edu sentences. The existing seven-language corpus coverage and seven contamination benchmarks remain; v1's reference to six languages was inconsistent with its own Table 3.

E2.justification: BM25, previously discussed only as related work, becomes an evaluated comparator in retrieval and paraphrase detection (v2 Tables 17–18). The original comparisons with infini-gram, infini-gram mini, and SoftMatcha are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include cold-cache controls, order-swapped GPT-5.4 judgments, manually prepared retrieval queries with precision/recall metrics, and 400 paraphrase-source tests. The pruning-latency sample increases from 400 to 2,000 queries. Reported English seven/eight-token proportions change from 7%/5% to 6%/6%, and cache clearing changes from CPU-cache terminology to OS page cache; these revisions do not establish reruns of all retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's pruning ablations and output-size/threshold analysis, v2 adds smooth-minimum versus plain-minimum quality comparisons, beta sensitivity examples, cold/hot-cache robustness checks, and empirical validation of theoretical assumptions with and without insertions/deletions. Appendix K.3 also revises the existing pruning-latency analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix M newly reports log-shifted geometric means to reduce outlier influence. Appendix K.3 explicitly increases the query sample for more reliable p99 estimation. This concerns statistical estimation and query sampling, not additional independent runs; confidence intervals and significance tests remain absent.

E6.justification: v2 adds retrieval, quality-judgment, cache, real-query, and assumption-validation results. New paraphrase P@1 is 84.3% for Ours, versus 74.5% for SoftMatcha and 82.8% for BM25 (Table 18). The main 278.17 ms latency and contamination totals remain, while lookup growth changes from 2.27 to 2.30 per token. Under the expanded query sample, Figure 15 plots higher latency with all pruning techniques, contradicting the accompanying speedup claim.

T1.justification: v1 derives a constant query-length bound from its corpus-occurrence hypothesis and a moderate-gamma condition. v2 replaces this reasoning with explicit growth assumptions permitting r >= 1 and the bound A*a*(1-r^m)/(1-r), constant only when r < 1. It revises the corpus-size proof and adds conditional analysis of adaptive thresholding and additional pruning in Appendix N.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the claimed applications from contamination detection to information retrieval and paraphrase detection. The theoretical contribution is qualified through revised conditional bounds and acknowledged non-decaying cases. The central claim of fast semantic search over trillion-scale corpora remains.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges that the occurrence-ratio intuition underlying v1's theory fails empirically and discusses linguistic constraints and examples with r >= 1 (Section 4; Appendix M). It adds substantive explanations of beta-dependent ranking tradeoffs and insertion-related grammatical errors affecting quality judgments. The existing multiword-semantics and resource limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds GPT-5.4 judging and paraphrasing prompts, query-selection and exclusion instructions, and settings for the new evaluations. Appendix D documents hyperparameter rationales, while Appendix H explains frequently accessed versus example-retrieval index storage. Its proposed SSD/HDD configuration is deployment guidance, rather than a newly tested hardware setup.

R1.justification: New citations support ORCAS, retrieval benchmarks, BM25, and query-length rationales. Earlier Heaps-law references to Baeza-Yates/Navarro and van Leijenhorst/van der Weide are removed. Table 2 refines lexical-semantic versus coarse-topic retrieval positioning, but the central relationship to SoftMatcha and the infini-gram systems remains.

P1.justification: Related work moves partly to Appendix A, problem formulation becomes Section 2.2, and the method is reorganized into six subsections separating building blocks, pruning, indexing, similarity, and thresholding. The introduction and theoretical exposition are extensively rewritten, and the evaluation, application, and appendix structures are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICML layout, restructures Table 2, moves the suffix-array diagram from v1's Appendix H into main-text Figure 3, resizes the contamination figure, and redraws Figure 15. It adds tables for downstream applications, cache conditions, real queries, quality judgments, beta sensitivity, and assumption validation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for practical usefulness through real-query, cold-cache, retrieval, and paraphrase evaluations, while exposing weaknesses in v1's occurrence-ratio rationale and making the theoretical conditions more explicit. Expanded experimental documentation and clearer organization improve assessability. Figure 15's contradiction with its pruning-speedup claim is a material regression, and geometric-mean checks do not fully validate expectation-based bounds. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in empirical support and theoretical transparency.
